records.table: Bushmills 10 Year Old Single Malt is triple distilled from malted barley alone in County Antrim and aged ten years in bourbon and sherry casks. It pours light and honeyed, with vanilla and a little chocolate, and shows a guest the soft Irish malt.
records.story: Bushmills prints 1608 on every bottle. As the house tells it, that is the year James I granted a local landowner a licence to distil in the district: a licence, not a distillery. The Old Bushmills Distillery Company was registered in 1784, and in 1885 a fire destroyed nearly all of the distillery, which was rebuilt. Prohibition in the United States closed the American market to Irish whiskey, and by 1972, when Bushmills joined Irish Distillers, it was one of two whiskey distilleries at work on the island. Pernod Ricard bought Irish Distillers in 1988, Diageo bought the distillery in 2005, and in 2014 Diageo agreed to hand Bushmills to Jose Cuervo in exchange for full ownership of Don Julio tequila. Through each change the malt stayed triple distilled from malted barley alone. For a bartender the 10 Year Old is the reference for the soft, triple distilled Irish malt, and the bottle to pour beside a peated Connemara.

records.table: Connemara Peated Single Malt is the smoky Irish whiskey: malted barley dried over peat fires, then double distilled at Cooley in County Louth. Expect sweet barley, peat smoke and baked apple; it is the answer when a guest asks whether Ireland makes a peated malt.
records.story: Cooley Distillery began in 1987, when a group led by its founder took over a former state plant for industrial alcohol at Riverstown, near Dundalk in County Louth. Converted to make whiskey, it began distilling in 1989, and it chose to distil its malt twice rather than three times. Connemara followed in 1996: a single malt made from barley dried over peat fires, which brought back an old Irish habit to a whiskey better known for soft, unpeated malt. Cooley was sold to Beam in 2012, and Suntory bought Beam in 2014. Through those changes Connemara kept its place as the peated malt of the Cooley range, sold without an age statement beside a 12 year old and a cask strength bottling. For a bartender it settles a question guests often ask: yes, Ireland makes smoky whiskey, and this is the bottle to pour when they want to taste it beside a soft Bushmills or an Islay malt.

records.table: The Tyrconnell Single Malt is a double distilled Irish malt from Cooley in County Louth, aged in bourbon casks and named for a Derry racehorse. It pours bright and citrusy, with lemon, green apple and honey: the Cooley malt to set beside smoky Connemara.
records.story: The name is older than the whiskey in the bottle. The Watt family ran a large distillery on Abbey Street in Derry, and the family's story is that in 1876 their horse The Tyrconnell won the National Produce Stakes at odds of a hundred to one, and that they named a whiskey for it to mark the win. The Watt distillery closed in the 1920s, and the name fell out of use. Cooley Distillery, founded in 1987 in a former state alcohol plant near Dundalk, brought it back as a single malt in the early 1990s; sources give the year as 1993 or 1994. Double distilled in pot stills and aged in bourbon casks, it became Cooley's plain malt, beside the peated Connemara that followed in 1996. Cooley was sold to Beam in 2012, and Suntory bought Beam in 2014. For a bartender the Tyrconnell carries two lessons: a revived Irish name need not come from its old distillery, and Cooley distils its malt twice where Bushmills distils three times.

records.story: Knappogue Castle is a tower house built in 1467 by the MacNamaras in the parish of Quin, County Clare. In 1966 a Houston businessman, a former Assistant Secretary of the United States Navy, bought it in ruins, and he and his wife, an architect, restored it. Around the same time, by the brand's account, he began buying casks of pot still whiskey from Irish distilleries, aged them further and bottled them under the castle's name. His son carried the label to the United States and other markets, and in 1998 founded the company that became Castle Brands, bringing the family's Knappogue Castle whiskey into it. Pernod Ricard agreed to buy Castle Brands in August 2019 and completed the purchase that October. The producer names no distillery, and accounts differ on whose stills made the malt over the years. For a bartender the bottle teaches that an Irish single malt label and the distillery behind it can be two different things, and that the castle on the label is a place to visit, not a distillery.

records.story: Walsh Whiskey began in County Carlow in 1999, when a husband and wife set up a company to make The Hot Irishman, an Irish Coffee liqueur. By the house's account The Irishman range of whiskeys had taken shape by 2006, led by single malt, and Writers' Tears followed. Like many Irish labels of those years it was bottled from whiskey made at a distillery the house did not own. In 2016 the founders opened a distillery on the Royal Oak estate in Carlow with Illva Saronno, the Italian maker of Disaronno, as an equal partner. In January 2019 the two parted over how to grow the business: the distillery passed to Illva and was renamed Royal Oak Distillery, and the brands stayed with Walsh. Amber Beverage Group bought Walsh Whiskey in November 2021. For a bartender The Irishman Single Malt shows that an Irish malt label may come from a house that buys and blends its whiskey, and that triple distillation and sherry wood are choices of style, not rules.
